2.4.1 GENERAL INTRODUCTION The term algae (Latin- seaweeds) have been used in a broad sense to aquatic, photosynthetic organisms. The group algae include an enormous group of plants of great biological importance and most primitive plants. They show a great variety. Some are considered to be a link between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

They are autotrophic, unicellular or multicellular, non-flowering and non-vascular plants. The algae are of great importance as primary producers of energy rich compounds in aquatic body. The branch of biology that deals with the study of algae is called phycology or algology. The person who is expert in algae is called phycologist. F.E. Fritsch is called father of phycology.
2.4.2 CHARACTERISTICS FEATURES OF ALGAE Some of the basic features of algae are given below:
1. The algae are aquatic, both marine and fresh water, occur on and within damp soil and moist stones, wood as well as in association with fungi and certain animals.

2. The body of algae is not differentiated into roots, stems or leaves, so, the body of the alga is known as a thallus. This term is used even if the plant is unicellular (e.g. Chlamydomonas). The body or thallus of multicellular algae ranges from simple floating colony of cells (e.g. Volvox), to filaments (e.g. Spirogyra) to sheets of cells (e.g. Ulva).
3. The body is usually covered with mucilage. 4. The cell wall is made up of cellulose. s 5. Photosynthetic pigments are chlorophyll and carotenoids. 6. The common reserve food material is starch.

7. Reproduction takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual method. 8. Vegetative reproduction is the most common type of reproduction. It takes place by

fragmentation, budding, etc. 9. Asexual reproduction takes place by means of spores. The spores are motile or nonmotile. 10. Sexual reproduction takes place by the fusion of gametes. It may be isogamous or anisogamous or oogamous. 11. An embryo stage is absent in life cycle of algae.
